title: VP versus VNP
formal:
Over the complex field \(\mathbb C\), do there exist integers \(B,k\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\), some arithmetic circuit with at most \(B(n+1)^k\) operation gates computes the permanent polynomial
\[\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^{n}x_{i,\sigma(i)}\ \in\mathbb C[x_{ij}:1\le i,j\le n]?\]
Circuits are division-free, have binary addition, subtraction and multiplication gates, allow arbitrary complex constants and unrestricted reuse, and compute exact formal polynomials. No uniform construction of the circuits is required. Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\), with the classes defined below? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
definitions:
Polynomial and parameter. For \(n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\), write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and let \(S_n\) be the set of bijections from \([n]\) to itself. The matrix \(X=(x_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}\) consists of \(n^2\) independent commuting indeterminates. The displayed sum has one product for each permutation; each product chooses one variable in each row and column. Its total degree is \(n\). The growing parameter in the size bound is the matrix dimension \(n\), not the number of monomials or the magnitude of a numerical input. The number of input variables is \(N=n^2\).

Circuit model. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with a distinguished output node. Each input node carries either one of the indeterminates or one exact constant from \(\mathbb C\). Each other node has two ordered incoming wires and a label \(+\), \(-\) or \(\times\); the same preceding node may feed both incoming wires. A node is evaluated in the commutative polynomial ring by applying its operation to the polynomials at its two predecessors. An input node itself may be the output. The circuit's size \(s(D)\) is the number of operation nodes; input nodes are not counted. A computed value may feed arbitrarily many subsequent nodes at no additional gate cost. Cancellations are allowed. Neither depth nor the degrees of intermediate polynomials are restricted. All constants are freely selected as part of the finite circuit and may depend on \(n\); their numerical bit lengths, descriptions or computability are not charged. Each arithmetic operation costs one gate. This is an arithmetic circuit measure, not a Turing-machine bit-time model. Input constants supply no operation other than their fixed field value: there are no bit-extraction, comparison, branching, oracle or division gates. Approximation and limits of circuits are also outside this model.

Exact computation and families. A circuit computes \(f\) when its output equals \(f\) as an element of the polynomial ring, meaning that every monomial has the same coefficient. Agreement at a selected finite set of matrices is not the correctness definition. Let \(c_{\mathbb C}(f)\) be the minimum size of such a circuit for \(f\). Every polynomial has a finite circuit, so this minimum is a nonnegative integer. In the main question the quantifier order is
\[\exists B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \forall n\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists D_n:\quad s(D_n)\le B(n+1)^k,\quad D_n\text{ computes }\operatorname{perm}_n.\]
The constants \(B,k\) are shared across all matrix dimensions. The circuits themselves may be unrelated from one dimension to the next: no machine, advice-generation procedure or polynomial-time algorithm for producing them is part of the assertion. Restricting constants to integers or rationals, or asking for a uniform family, would change this selected model.

Complexity classes. A sequence \(a(n)\) of nonnegative integers is polynomially bounded if some integers \(B,k\ge1\) satisfy \(a(n)\le B(n+1)^k\) for every \(n\ge1\). A polynomial family is a sequence \((m(n),f_n)_{n\ge1}\) with \(m(n)\ge0\) and \(f_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)}]\); both \(m(n)\) and the total degree of \(f_n\) must be polynomially bounded. Total degree is the largest sum of exponents of a monomial with nonzero coefficient; for this boundedness condition give the zero polynomial degree zero. The family lies in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\) if \(c_{\mathbb C}(f_n)\) is polynomially bounded as well, using the circuit model above. These are bounds on the resulting polynomials, not extra syntactic degree bounds at circuit gates.

Such a family lies in \(\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\) if there are a polynomially bounded witness length \(w(n)\in\mathbb N\) and a family
\[g_n\in\mathbb C[x_1,\ldots,x_{m(n)},y_1,\ldots,y_{w(n)}]\]
in \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\), with combined variable counts and total degrees polynomially bounded in \(n\), such that
\[f_n(x)=\sum_{a\in\{0,1\}^{w(n)}}g_n(x,a).\]
Each Boolean witness is embedded into \(\mathbb C^{w(n)}\) using the field elements zero and one; the sum is a finite algebraic sum over exactly those witnesses, not an existential quantifier and not a sum over all complex tuples. If \(w(n)=0\), there is one empty witness, so \(\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}\subseteq\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}\). No uniformity is imposed on these families or their circuit constants. Class equality means equality of these collections of polynomial families.
answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the stated existence proposition or its logical negation. A positive answer must establish common integers \(B,k\ge1\) and an appropriate finite circuit for every \(n\), with exact polynomial identity and the size bound in this model. A uniform construction is sufficient but is not required. A negative answer must prove
\[\forall B,k\in\mathbb N_{>0}\ \exists n\in\mathbb N_{>0}:\quad c_{\mathbb C}(\operatorname{perm}_n)>B(n+1)^k.\]
Equivalently, the violating dimension can be required to exceed any specified lower threshold, since finitely many exceptions can be absorbed into the coefficient \(B\). The lower bound must cover every finite circuit with arbitrary complex constants, cancellations and reuse. A result proved via the class-equality formulation must include the equivalence to this concrete permanent target. A fixed polynomial lower bound, even superlinear in \(n^2\), is insufficient to prove the negation. Lower bounds confined to formulas, monotone circuits, fixed depth, or superpolynomial determinantal complexity do not by themselves establish the required general-circuit separation. A numerical approximation scheme, a border-limit construction, or a result only over another field does not supply the exact circuits quantified here.
why: This is the central equality question for general arithmetic computation. It asks whether a polynomial-size algebraic computation can always absorb a sum over exponentially many Boolean witnesses, with the permanent serving as a complete concrete target. A separation would establish a general limitation despite arbitrary constants, cancellations and reuse; equality would give polynomial-size circuits for every polynomial family in VNP.

importance.reason: A foundational separation for general arithmetic circuits, with a complete concrete target in the permanent and consequences across algebraic complexity and explicit lower-bound constructions.

progress.text: Ryser’s identity yields exponential-size permanent formulas, for example \(O(n^2 2^n)\) operations.

Valiant proves permanent completeness under polynomial-size projections in characteristic different from two. The modern formulation makes polynomial-size permanent circuits equivalent to VP=VNP over C.
Limaye–Srinivasan–Tavenas prove superpolynomial lower bounds for every fixed depth in characteristic zero; the journal version appears in 2025. Unrestricted circuits are outside that lower bound.

OpenAI reports \(\Omega(n^2\log\log n)\) general division-free circuit size and \(\Omega(n^4/\log n)\) formula size for the permanent, with released Lean certificates. These polynomial lower bounds do not settle VP versus VNP; certificates were not replayed in this review.
Narayanan’s July-submitted manuscript is published on ECCC with improved sublogarithmic-depth lower bounds and exponential-degree elusive curves; its parameters do not yield the full separation.
Kudria–Luo–Majid report a subexponential multiplicative approximation factor in deterministic polynomial bit time for nonnegative rational matrices, a distinct numerical target.

status_note: Checked through 16 September 2026. No polynomial-size general permanent circuits or matching superpolynomial lower bound were found in the bounded primary-source review. The August OpenAI chapter reports a general permanent lower bound of order n^2 log log n and formula lower bounds, with released Lean certificates; these remain polynomial and the certificates were not independently replayed here. Narayanan’s depth/degree-qualified results and the September numerical approximation theorem have different guarantees. The full VP-versus-VNP question over C remains source-open in the inspected literature.

context_blocks.text: The permanent of a matrix sums the weights of its perfect matchings when rows and columns form the two sides of a bipartite graph. For a zero-one matrix it counts perfect matchings. Already in dimension two, \(\operatorname{perm}_2(X)=x_{11}x_{22}+x_{12}x_{21}\), while the determinant subtracts the second product. This card concerns the symbolic polynomial for all complex inputs.

The determinant contains the same permutation products with signs, yet has polynomial-size division-free circuits. Thus factorially many displayed terms do not force factorial circuit size. Reusing expressions and canceling terms are central powers of the model. Counting perfect matchings on binary inputs is a related Boolean counting problem, but that bit-complexity problem is not the same as allowing arbitrary complex constants at unit arithmetic cost.

Valiant’s completeness theorem makes the permanent universal for \(\mathrm{VNP}\) over fields of characteristic different from two. Each VNP family can be obtained from a polynomially larger permanent by substituting variables and field constants. This establishes the equivalence in the question over \(\mathbb C\). The field choice matters: in characteristic two the permanent and determinant coincide.

Ryser’s identity gives an exponential-size upper bound, including formulas using \(O(n^2 2^n)\) arithmetic operations. In contrast, a positive answer here requires one fixed polynomial bound for all dimensions. A formula is a circuit whose intermediate results cannot be shared; forbidding reuse can substantially increase the needed size.

Limaye, Srinivasan and Tavenas proved superpolynomial lower bounds for every constant circuit depth over characteristic-zero fields. Their hard polynomial is an iterated matrix product entry, which itself has polynomial-size unrestricted circuits. The low-depth theorem therefore illustrates the power of removing a depth restriction rather than proving VP different from VNP. The result first appeared in 2021 and was published in the Journal of the ACM in 2025.

The 1 August 2026 OpenAI manuscript reports a lower bound \(\Omega(n^2\log\log n)\) for unrestricted division-free circuits computing the permanent, and \(\Omega(n^4/\log n)\) for formulas, including formulas with valid divisions. The circuit model in Chapter 5 matches this card, but the bound is still polynomial in matrix dimension and hence does not separate VP and VNP. The release supplies Lean certificates; this review checked the mathematical statements and repository description without replaying or independently auditing those certificates.

Narayanan’s work, published on ECCC on 9 August 2026 after a July submission, reports improved superlinear lower bounds for certain sublogarithmic depths and explicit elusive curves of exponential degree. The manuscript explicitly explains that its current parameters do not establish VP different from VNP. These are results with stated depth and degree qualifications, not a general superpolynomial permanent lower bound.

A determinantal representation expresses a polynomial as \(\det A(x)\), where every matrix entry is an affine linear form in its variables. Its minimum matrix dimension measures a more restricted representation than an arbitrary arithmetic circuit. A superpolynomial bound on that dimension alone does not settle this card; polynomial-size general circuits can be simulated by determinantal representations of quasipolynomial size. Exact representation must also be distinguished from taking limits of such representations.

Kudria, Luo and Majid’s 9 September 2026 preprint gives deterministic polynomial bit-time approximation of the permanent of nonnegative rational matrices within a factor \(\exp(O(n(\log\log n)^2/\log n))\). This is a recent algorithmic advance for numerical approximate counting. Its input restriction and multiplicative-error guarantee do not give exact formal-polynomial circuits over \(\mathbb C\).

sentences: The permanent sums one product of matrix variables for each permutation of the columns.
The question is whether exact division-free arithmetic circuits over the complex numbers compute these polynomials with one polynomial size bound for all matrix dimensions.
The selected model permits arbitrary complex constants, cancellations, unrestricted reuse and a different circuit at each dimension without a uniform generator.
A complete Lean proof must establish such circuits or rule out every polynomial size bound, equivalently settling VP versus VNP in this model.
The checked August polynomial lower bounds, constant-depth separations and September numerical approximation result do not settle the required general exact-circuit question.

source_formulation.interpretation: Retained the selected field C, arbitrary-constant nonuniform binary arithmetic circuits and exact permanent target. Operation-gate size differs from the book’s wire count only by the usual bounded-fan-in conversion, preserving polynomial size. The class definitions spell out polynomial variable/degree bounds and Boolean witness summation; no Turing bit-cost, effective circuit generator, syntactic degree restriction or border closure is introduced.
